label: Jewish funeral and shiva
serviceTimelineNote: Jewish tradition asks for burial quickly — usually within 24 to 48 hours, sometimes the same day. The funeral itself is short and plain by design. Shiva, the seven days of mourning at home that follow, is where remembering happens slowly, with visitors, food, and stories. There is far more time than the first day makes it feel like.

mediaPlacement.guidance: The service is deliberately simple: psalms, a eulogy (hesped), and the burial. Photo slideshows are not usually part of it, and there is rarely time to make one before the funeral anyway. Please do not spend the first day trying.

This is where photographs belong. Many families put out framed pictures and photo albums, or run a quiet loop on a laptop or television in the corner of the room. Visitors come to talk about the person who died — the photos give them somewhere to start.

Thirty days after the burial (shloshim), and again at the unveiling of the headstone near the first anniversary, families often gather again. A finished tribute video is very welcome at those gatherings, and you will have had time to make it properly.

musicGuidance: Music is traditionally minimal or absent at the funeral itself, and during shiva many families keep the house quiet. Take your lead from the rabbi or the funeral home.
For a video shown at shloshim or a later memorial, gentle instrumental music is the safest and usually the loveliest choice.
If you would like their favourite songs, save them for a family gathering rather than the funeral or the shiva house.

interviewAdjustments.note: Family history often carries migration, name changes, and relatives lost. Ask openly, follow where the person leads, and let them stop.
Ask about practice and belonging — the shul, the holidays they hosted, the recipes, the community work — rather than about belief in the abstract.

checklistExtras: Do nothing about video in the first day or two. Gathering photos can wait until after the burial.
Ask family to send photos to the shared link during shiva — visitors often have pictures nobody else has.
Ask the rabbi or funeral home what they suggest for the service; they will answer plainly and quickly.
deliveryNotes: For shiva, a laptop or a television with a USB port in the corner of the room is usually all you need.
For a shloshim or first-anniversary gathering, bring the video on a USB stick formatted FAT32 or exFAT, and send a copy to the venue ahead of time.

orderOfService.note: The chapel or graveside fills quietly
The eulogy, given by the rabbi or by family

Times for the days that follow

readings.title: Psalm 23 — The Lord is my shepherd
readings.source: Psalm 23, Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917 — public domain
readings.text: The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures; He leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreth my soul; He guideth me in straight paths for His name's sake. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for Thou art with me; Thy rod and Thy staff, they comfort me. Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies; Thou hast anointed my head with oil; my cup runneth over. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life; and I shall dwell in the house of the Lord for ever.

readings.title: To every thing there is a season
readings.source: Ecclesiastes 3:1–4, Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917 — public domain
readings.text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted; a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up; a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance.

readings.title: A woman of valour
readings.source: Proverbs 31:10, 25–29, Jewish Publication Society translation, 1917 — public domain. Often read for a mother or grandmother.
readings.text: A woman of valour who can find? For her price is far above rubies. Strength and dignity are her clothing; and she laugheth at the time to come. She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and the law of kindness is on her tongue. She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness. Her children rise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.

readings.title: Mourner's Kaddish
readings.source: Traditional Aramaic prayer. Printed in Hebrew and transliteration by the funeral home or synagogue — ask them for the sheet they use.
